title: The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
outcomes: Explain the meaning and characteristics of negotiable instruments and identify bearer and order instruments.
Define and distinguish promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques (including electronic and truncated cheques), and test whether an instrument is valid.
Classify instruments as inland or foreign, inchoate or ambiguous, and explain negotiation by delivery and by indorsement and delivery.
Apply the provisions on dishonour of cheques (Sections 138–140), presentment (Sections 61–77) and compensation (Section 117) to problems.

meta.exam_tip: Section 138 problems with dates, validity of promissory notes and inland/foreign classification are frequent. Show each time limit against the dates; test each essential against the wording of the instrument.

concepts.title: Meaning and characteristics of negotiable instruments (Section 13)
body: A negotiable instrument is a written document that can be passed freely from hand to hand — by delivery, or by indorsement and delivery — so that a person who takes it in good faith and for value gets a good title to it.

The Act does not give a full definition. Section 13 says that a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable either to order or to bearer is a negotiable instrument. Other documents such as hundis, treasury bills, bearer debentures and (for some purposes) bills of lading and delivery orders are treated as negotiable by mercantile custom or usage.

Payable to order: when it is expressed to be so payable, or is payable to a particular person without words forbidding transfer. Payable to bearer: when it says so (e.g. "pay bearer"), or when the only or last indorsement on it is in blank.

Characteristics: (1) in writing; (2) signed by the maker/drawer; (3) freely transferable; (4) the holder in due course gets a title free from defects of earlier parties; (5) can be transferred any number of times until paid; (6) contains an unconditional promise or order to pay money only; (7) the amount, the time of payment and the payee must be certain; (8) it must be delivered — merely writing it creates no liability.
concepts.analogy: A negotiable instrument is like a currency note made to order: it travels from person to person, and an honest taker is protected even if someone earlier in the chain had a weak claim.
concepts.work: CAs see these instruments daily — post-dated cheques from customers, trade bills discounted with banks, promissory notes behind loans. Knowing which is valid and transferable decides whether a receivable is properly evidenced and recoverable.

concepts.title: Promissory note (Section 4)
body: A promissory note is a written document — other than a bank note or currency note — in which the maker, over his signature, undertakes without any condition to pay a fixed amount of money (and nothing else) to a definite person, to that person's order, or to the bearer. Parties: the maker (who promises and signs — the debtor) and the payee.

Essentials: (a) in writing — an oral promise is not enough; (b) an express promise to pay — a mere acknowledgment of a debt ("I owe you ₹5,000") is not a note; (c) the promise must be definite and unconditional — payment dependent on an uncertain event makes it invalid, but an event that is bound to happen (e.g. a person's death) does not make it conditional; (d) signed by the maker; (e) to pay money only — not money plus goods; (f) a certain sum — "₹20,000 with interest at 10% a year" is certain, "₹20,000 and whatever else I may owe" is not; (g) maker and payee must be certain and different persons; (h) duly stamped under the Indian Stamp Act, with the stamp cancelled.
Under Section 31 of the RBI Act, 1934, only the RBI (or the Central Government, as allowed) can issue a promissory note payable to bearer; a private person's note cannot be payable to bearer.
concepts.analogy: A promissory note is a written "I will pay you" — the borrower makes the promise himself.
concepts.work: Banks and NBFCs take demand promissory notes as loan documents; an auditor checks that the note is unconditional, for a certain sum, signed and properly stamped — otherwise its evidentiary value is weak.

concepts.title: Bill of exchange (Section 5)
body: A bill of exchange is a written, signed document in which the maker (drawer) instructs, without condition, a definite person (drawee) to pay a fixed amount of money — money alone — to a definite person, to that person's order, or to the bearer.

Parties: the drawer (who makes the bill — usually the creditor); the drawee (on whom it is drawn and who is ordered to pay — becomes the acceptor once he accepts, and his liability is then primary and unconditional); and the payee (to whom payment is to be made — may be the drawer himself or a third person). A "drawee in case of need" is a person named in the bill or an indorsement to be approached if the drawee does not pay.

Essentials: in writing; an express order to pay; definite and unconditional; signed by the drawer; drawer, drawee and payee certain (one person may fill two roles, but there must be at least two distinct persons); certain sum; money only; stamped. Under the RBI Act a bill cannot be made payable to bearer on demand, though a demand bill payable to a named person or order is valid.

Working of a trade bill: a seller supplies goods on credit, draws a bill on the buyer; the buyer accepts it; on maturity the holder presents it to the buyer for payment. Meanwhile the seller may discount it with a bank or indorse it to his own creditor.

blocks.title: Promissory note vs bill of exchange

concepts.analogy: A promissory note is "I will pay you"; a bill of exchange is "You (drawee) pay him (payee)" — signed by the person giving the order.
concepts.work: Bill discounting and LC-backed bills are common in working-capital finance. CAs verify acceptance, maturity dates and the bank's recourse against the drawer when assessing contingent liabilities.

concepts.title: Cheque (Section 6)
body: A cheque is a species of bill of exchange: it is always drawn on a named (specified) banker and is always payable on demand. The definition also covers a cheque in electronic form and the electronic image of a truncated cheque.

An electronic-form cheque is created on a computer resource and authenticated within a secure system by a digital signature (biometric signature optional) using an asymmetric crypto system, or by an electronic signature. A truncated cheque is one whose physical movement is stopped during clearing and replaced by an electronic image, by the clearing house or the paying or collecting bank. The clearing house means one managed or recognised by the RBI. The technical terms carry their Information Technology Act, 2000 meanings.
Section 3 extends the word "banker" to anyone carrying on banking and to a post office savings bank.

Parties: drawer (the account holder who writes it — his liability is primary but conditional on presentment), drawee (always a specified bank), and payee (may be the drawer himself or another person).
So every cheque is a bill of exchange, with two extra features — always drawn on a specified banker and always payable on demand; but not every bill is a cheque.
concepts.analogy: A cheque is a bill of exchange with a fixed address (a specified bank) and no waiting period (always on demand).
concepts.work: Under CTS (cheque truncation), only images travel between banks. Cash-flow and bank-reconciliation work depends on knowing when a cheque is "presented" and when it can be treated as dishonoured.

concepts.title: Classification: bearer/order, inland/foreign, inchoate, ambiguous
body: Bearer instrument: payee's name left blank, or payable to a named person "or bearer", or the last indorsement is in blank — negotiated by mere delivery. Order instrument: payable to a person, to a person or his order, or to the order of a person, or the last indorsement is in full — negotiated by indorsement and delivery.

Inland instrument (Section 11): a note, bill or cheque drawn or made in India and either made payable in India or drawn upon a person resident in India. It stays inland even if indorsed abroad. Foreign instrument (Section 12): any instrument that is not inland.

Section 134: in the absence of a contrary contract, a maker or drawer of a foreign instrument answers according to the law of the country where he made it, while an acceptor or indorser answers according to the law of the country where it is payable.

Inchoate instrument (Section 20): a person who signs and delivers a paper stamped as required by law, wholly blank or containing an incomplete instrument, gives the holder prima facie authority to complete it for any amount not exceeding what the stamp covers. He is liable to a holder in due course for the amount filled in (within the stamp); a holder other than a holder in due course cannot recover more than the signer intended. The rule rests on estoppel, and it needs delivery — a blank paper stolen from the signer's drawer creates no liability.

Ambiguous instrument (Section 17): where an instrument may be read either as a promissory note or as a bill, the holder may elect to treat it as either; once he chooses, it is treated that way thereafter.

blocks.title: Inland or foreign? (Sections 11 and 12)

concepts.analogy: An inchoate instrument is a signed blank cheque leaf: the signer has trusted the holder to fill it in, and an innocent later holder may hold him to what was filled in.
concepts.work: Security cheques handed over blank (signed) to lenders and suppliers are common; CAs advising clients point out that a holder in due course may enforce the amount filled in, within the law.

concepts.title: Negotiation (Sections 14, 46, 47, 48, 57)
body: Section 14: when an instrument is transferred to a person so as to make him its holder, it is negotiated. Negotiation transfers ownership of the instrument.

Section 47: an instrument payable to bearer is negotiated by delivery. Exception: if it was handed over on the understanding that it would operate only when some event occurs, it cannot be negotiated until that event happens — though a holder for value who did not know of the condition is protected. Section 48: an instrument payable to order is negotiated by the holder by indorsement and delivery. Both are subject to Section 58 (instruments obtained unlawfully or for unlawful consideration).

Section 46 — delivery is essential, both when making/drawing and when negotiating. It must be voluntary and meant to pass the property. Delivery may be actual (physical handing over) or constructive (to the transferee's agent, clerk or servant, or where the indorser, after indorsing, holds it as the indorsee's agent). Until delivery, the contract on the instrument is incomplete and revocable. As between immediate parties (and against a holder who is not a holder in due course), it may be shown that delivery was conditional or for a special purpose only.
Section 57: where the deceased had indorsed an order instrument but died before handing it over, his legal representative cannot complete the negotiation simply by delivering it.
concepts.analogy: Indorsing a cheque without handing it over is like writing a gift card and leaving it in your drawer — nothing has been given yet.
concepts.work: In receivable audits, an indorsed-but-undelivered bill found in a client's safe is still the client's asset; the indorsee has no rights in it yet.

concepts.title: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)
body: Section 138: where a cheque drawn by a person on his account with a banker, for paying money to another person towards discharge (in whole or part) of a debt or other liability, is returned unpaid because the balance is insufficient or it exceeds the arrangement (overdraft limit) agreed with the bank, the drawer is deemed to have committed an offence — punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both.

Conditions: (a) the cheque was presented within three months of its date or within its validity period, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or holder in due course gave the drawer a written notice demanding payment within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour from the bank; and (c) the drawer failed to pay within 15 days of receiving the notice. "Debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable one — so cheques given as gifts, donations, mere security without an existing liability, for a moral obligation or for an illegal purpose fall outside Section 138.

A post-dated cheque counts as drawn on the date it bears; dishonour because the drawer stopped payment (where funds were also inadequate, or with intent to avoid payment) can also attract Section 138.

Section 139: it is presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder received the cheque for discharge of a debt or liability — a rebuttable presumption that puts the burden on the accused. Section 140: it is no defence that the drawer had no reason to believe, when issuing the cheque, that it might be dishonoured.
concepts.analogy: The 30 + 15 rule: 30 days for the payee to send the demand, then 15 days of grace for the drawer to pay before the offence is complete.
concepts.work: Credit teams track dishonour memos and notice dates precisely; a CA reviewing recovery cases checks that the 3-month, 30-day and 15-day limits were met, otherwise the criminal remedy is lost and only a civil suit remains.

concepts.title: Presentment of instruments (Sections 61 to 77)
body: For acceptance (Section 61): a bill payable after sight has to be shown to the drawee for his acceptance — by someone entitled to ask for it, within a reasonable period from the date of drawing, during business hours on a working day — provided the drawee can be traced after reasonable search. Failing this, no party is liable to the person in default. If the drawee cannot be found, the bill is dishonoured. Presentment by registered post is enough where agreement or usage allows. Section 62: a note payable a fixed period after sight must likewise be shown to the maker for sight within a reasonable time. Section 63: the drawee may ask for 48 hours (excluding public holidays) to decide whether to accept.

For payment (Section 64): the holder must present a note to its maker, a bill to its acceptor and a cheque to the drawee bank; if he does not, the other parties are released as against him. No presentment is needed to charge the maker of a demand note not payable at a specified place. For a truncated cheque, the drawee bank may ask for further information or, if it suspects fraud, forgery, tampering or destruction, for the physical cheque itself.

Time and place: during usual business hours, and at a bank within banking hours (Section 65); instruments payable after date or sight — at maturity (Section 66); instalment notes — on the third day after each instalment date (Section 67); at the specified place where so payable (Sections 68, 69); else at the place of business or usual residence of the maker/drawee/acceptor (Section 70); if none is known, to him personally wherever found (Section 71).

Cheques: to charge the drawer, present before the drawer's relationship with the bank changes to his prejudice (Section 72); to charge others, within a reasonable time after delivery by them (Section 73). Demand instruments — within a reasonable time after the holder receives them (Section 74). Presentment may be to an authorised agent, legal representative of a deceased, or assignee of an insolvent (Section 75). Delay beyond the holder's control is excused (Section 75A).

Presentment unnecessary (Section 76): if the maker/drawee/acceptor intentionally prevents it, closes his business place on a business day, no one attends at the specified place, or he cannot be found; against a party who has agreed to pay despite non-presentment; against a party who, after maturity and knowing of non-presentment, makes part payment, promises to pay or otherwise waives it; and against the drawer who could suffer no damage from non-presentment. Section 77: a bank that negligently deals with a bill accepted payable there and dishonoured must compensate the holder.
concepts.analogy: Presentment is knocking on the right door at the right time; skip it and the people standing behind the main debtor (drawer, indorsers) can walk away.
concepts.work: Treasury and bank-reconciliation teams follow presentment rules for post-dated cheques and bills under collection; delay may discharge indorsers and weaken recovery.

concepts.title: Rules of compensation on dishonour (Section 117)
body: Compensation payable by a party liable to the holder or an indorsee on dishonour of a note, bill or cheque is determined as follows:

(a) the holder recovers what is due on the instrument together with the costs reasonably spent on presenting, noting and protesting it; (b) where the party charged resides somewhere other than the place of payment, the holder recovers that sum converted at the prevailing exchange rate between the two places;

(c) an indorser who was liable and has paid recovers what he paid, plus interest at 18% a year running from the day he paid till the day the money is tendered or realised, plus every expense the dishonour and payment caused him; (d) if he and the party charged live in different places, the prevailing exchange rate applies;

(e) the person due compensation may draw a bill, payable at sight or on demand, on the party liable for the amount due plus expenses, accompanied by the dishonoured instrument and protest (if any); if that bill is dishonoured, compensation is payable on it in the same way.
concepts.analogy: Section 117 is the bill for the clean-up after a bounced instrument: the amount, the costs and — for an indorser who paid — interest at 18%.
concepts.work: When a client indorser has paid a dishonoured bill, the CA computes the recoverable amount — principal, noting charges and 18% interest — and books it as a claim against prior parties.

illustrations.title: Is it a valid promissory note?
illustrations.q: State with reasons whether each is a valid promissory note: (a) "I owe Ramesh ₹15,000. — Suresh." (b) "I promise to pay Ramesh ₹15,000 on demand for value received. — Suresh." (c) "I promise to pay Ramesh ₹15,000 when I get a government job. — Suresh." (d) "I promise to pay Ramesh ₹15,000 and hand over my scooter on 1 July. — Suresh." (e) "I promise to pay Ramesh ₹15,000 thirty days after the death of my uncle Mohan. — Suresh." (f) "I promise to pay Ramesh ₹15,000 with interest at 12% a year, on 31 December. — Suresh."

Valid?
Reason
rows: Mere acknowledgment of debt — no promise to pay
Express, unconditional promise to pay a certain sum to a certain person, signed
Conditional — getting a government job is uncertain
Promise is not to pay money only (scooter also)
Death is certain to happen, only its time is uncertain — the promise is not conditional
Sum with stated interest is certain (can be calculated)

solution.text: All valid notes must also be duly stamped under the Indian Stamp Act.

illustrations.title: Inland or foreign?
illustrations.q: Classify: (a) a bill drawn in Ahmedabad on a merchant resident in Surat, stated to be payable in Hong Kong; (b) a bill drawn in Ahmedabad on a merchant in Hong Kong and accepted payable in Hong Kong; (c) a cheque drawn in Kolkata on a Kolkata bank, indorsed later in Paris; (d) a note made in Toronto payable in Bengaluru.

solution.provision: Section 11: an instrument drawn or made in India and either payable in India or drawn on a person resident in India is inland; it remains inland even if indorsed abroad. Section 12: any other instrument is foreign.
solution.facts: (a) Drawn in India on a person resident in India. (b) Drawn in India, but on a person abroad and payable abroad. (c) Drawn in India on a bank in India; indorsed abroad. (d) Made outside India.
solution.analysis: (a) satisfies the "drawn upon a person resident in India" limb. (b) satisfies neither limb. (c) satisfies both limbs; foreign indorsement is irrelevant. (d) is not made in India at all.

illustrations.title: Indorsed but not delivered
illustrations.q: Kabir holds a bill payable to his order for ₹1,20,000. He indorses it in favour of Leela and keeps it in his locker, intending to hand it over the next day. Kabir dies that night. Leela finds the bill among his papers when his family opens the locker. Kabir's son offers to hand the bill to Leela. Is Leela the holder?

solution.provision: Section 48: an order instrument is negotiated by indorsement and delivery. Section 46: delivery is essential; until then the transaction is incomplete and revocable. Section 57: a legal representative cannot negotiate by mere delivery an order instrument indorsed but not delivered by the deceased.
solution.facts: Kabir indorsed the bill to Leela but never delivered it. After his death his son wishes to hand it over.
solution.analysis: Negotiation was incomplete for want of delivery. The son, as legal representative, cannot complete it by delivery under Section 57.
solution.conclusion: Leela is not the holder of the bill; it remains part of Kabir's estate.

illustrations.title: Cheque bounce: counting the days (Section 138)
illustrations.q: On 5 March, Arora Traders received from Mittal & Co. a cheque dated 5 March for ₹3,50,000 towards the price of goods supplied. It was presented on 28 April and returned on 30 April marked "funds insufficient". Arora received the bank's return memo on 2 May and sent a demand notice, which Mittal received on 9 May. Mittal has not paid. (a) Was the cheque presented in time? (b) By when should the notice have been sent? (c) When does the offence become complete? (d) What is the maximum punishment?

solution.provision: Section 138: the dishonour of a cheque issued for a legally enforceable debt, for insufficiency of funds, is an offence if (a) it is presented within three months of its date or within its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee gives written notice of demand within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour; and (c) the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receiving the notice. Punishment: imprisonment up to two years, or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both.
solution.facts: Cheque dated 5 March; presented 28 April; payee informed 2 May; notice received by drawer 9 May; no payment. The cheque was for the price of goods — a legally enforceable debt.
solution.analysis: (a) 28 April is within three months of 5 March. (b) 30 days from 2 May end on 1 June; the notice was in time. (c) 15 days from 9 May end on 24 May; on default the cause of action arises on 25 May. (d) Twice ₹3,50,000 = ₹7,00,000.
solution.conclusion: All conditions are met. Mittal & Co. commits an offence under Section 138 on default after 24 May; punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or fine up to ₹7,00,000, or both.

head: Step
Rule
Date
rows: 3 months from cheque date / validity, whichever earlier
Till early June (presented 28 April — in time)
15 days from receipt of notice (9 May)

checks.label: last day (June) for notice: 30 days from 2 May
last day (May) for drawer to pay: 15 days from receipt of notice
cause of action arises the next day (May)

illustrations.title: Indorser's compensation (Section 117)
illustrations.q: A bill for ₹2,40,000 drawn by Pai and indorsed by Qadir to Rana is dishonoured by the acceptor at maturity. Rana claims from Qadir, who pays ₹2,40,000 on 1 July. Qadir spends ₹1,800 on noting and other costs due to the dishonour. He recovers from Pai (the drawer) on 1 December. How much can Qadir claim from Pai?

solution.provision: Section 117(c): a liable indorser who has paid may recover the sum paid, interest on it at 18% a year from his payment date till tender or realisation, and all expenses flowing from the dishonour and payment.
solution.facts: Qadir paid ₹2,40,000 on 1 July and incurred ₹1,800 expenses. Recovery is made on 1 December — 5 months later.

checks.label: interest at 18% p.a. for 5 months on amount paid by indorser

illustrations.title: A signed blank cheque leaf (Section 20)
illustrations.q: Varun signs a blank cheque leaf and gives it to his manager, Deepa, telling her to fill in up to ₹50,000 for a supplier. Deepa fills in ₹1,50,000 in favour of her friend Ishaan, who knows of the limit, and Ishaan indorses it to Jatin, who takes it in good faith for value without any knowledge. The cheque is dishonoured. Can Ishaan or Jatin recover ₹1,50,000 from Varun?

solution.provision: Section 20: a person who signs and delivers a blank or incomplete instrument gives prima facie authority to the holder to complete it. He is liable to a holder in due course for the amount filled in; but no one other than a holder in due course can recover more than the amount intended by him. (A cheque needs no stamp, so the stamp ceiling does not arise; courts apply the same principle to signed blank cheques.)
solution.facts: Varun signed and delivered a blank cheque, authorising up to ₹50,000. Deepa filled in ₹1,50,000. Ishaan knew of the limit; Jatin took the cheque in good faith, for value, without notice.
solution.analysis: Ishaan is not a holder in due course (he knew of the limit), so he can recover at most what Varun intended — ₹50,000. Jatin is a holder in due course; Varun is estopped from denying the amount as against him.
solution.conclusion: Jatin can recover ₹1,50,000 from Varun. Ishaan, had he sued, could have recovered only ₹50,000. Varun may in turn proceed against Deepa.

jobs.title: Recovering a bounced customer cheque
jobs.role: CA in industry, receivables head of a distribution company
jobs.situation: A customer's cheque for ₹4.8 lakh, given for goods supplied, has bounced for "insufficient funds". The sales team wants to "wait and see".
steps: Note the date of the bank's return memo — the 30-day clock for the demand notice starts on receiving that information.
Send a written demand notice by a mode that gives proof of delivery, stating the cheque details and amount.
Track 15 days from the customer's receipt of the notice; if unpaid, the offence is complete and a complaint can be filed (within one month of the cause of action, under Section 142).
In the books: keep the receivable, assess recoverability, and disclose litigation if material.
jobs.takeaway: Section 138 is a powerful recovery tool, but only if the 3-month, 30-day and 15-day limits are strictly met.
jobs.think: The customer argues that he believed funds would be available when he issued the cheque. Is that a defence?
jobs.answer: No. Section 140 says it is no defence that the drawer had no reason to believe the cheque might be dishonoured.

jobs.title: Reviewing promissory notes in a loan file
jobs.role: Statutory branch auditor of a bank
jobs.situation: Loan files contain demand promissory notes; some are unstamped, one says "I promise to pay ₹10 lakh and such further sums as the bank may advance".
steps: Check the essentials of Section 4: unconditional promise, certain sum, money only, signed, maker and payee certain.
The note with "such further sums" fails the "certain sum" test — flag it.
Unstamped or improperly stamped notes have weak evidentiary value — recommend fresh documentation.
Report documentation deficiencies in the branch audit report.
jobs.takeaway: A defect in the note can turn a secured-looking file into a documentation risk.

jobs.title: Year-end bills receivable
jobs.role: Article assistant on a statutory audit
jobs.situation: The client holds accepted trade bills; one bill was indorsed to a supplier but is still in the client's safe on 31 March.
steps: Apply Section 46: without delivery, negotiation is incomplete, so the bill is still the client's asset.
Check maturity dates and whether bills were presented for payment on time (Section 66) to keep the drawers/indorsers liable.
For discounted bills not yet matured, disclose the contingent liability to the bank.
jobs.takeaway: Delivery decides ownership of the bill; presentment decides whether secondary parties remain liable.

mcqs.q: Section 13 of the Negotiable Instruments Act names which instruments as negotiable instruments?
options: Promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques
Promissory notes, bills of exchange and hundis
Cheques, bank drafts and treasury bills
Bills of lading, delivery orders and cheques
mcqs.explain: Section 13 names only three negotiable instruments: promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques, payable either to order or to bearer. Hundis, bank drafts and treasury bills may be negotiable by custom or usage, but Section 13 does not name them. The hundi answer is the trap because hundis are a famous Indian instrument. Bills of lading are documents of title to goods, not negotiable instruments under this Act. In practice: bankers treat demand drafts like cheques by usage, while the Act itself names only these three.
mcqs.topic: Meaning and characteristics of negotiable instruments (Section 13)

mcqs.q: An instrument becomes payable to bearer when:
options: The only or last indorsement on it is in blank
It is payable to a named person without words forbidding transfer
The last indorsement is in full
mcqs.explain: Under the Explanation to Section 13, a note, bill or cheque is payable to bearer when it is expressed to be so payable, or when the only or last indorsement on it is an indorsement in blank (just the indorser's signature). Anyone holding it can then claim payment. "Last indorsement in full" is the trap: a full indorsement names the indorsee, so the instrument stays payable to order. Crossing affects how a cheque is paid, not whether it is bearer. In practice: a cheque signed on the back without naming anyone is risky, because anyone finding it becomes the holder.
mcqs.topic: Meaning and characteristics of negotiable instruments (Section 13)

mcqs.q: "I.O.U. ₹8,000" signed by the debtor is:
options: Not a promissory note — no promise to pay
mcqs.explain: Section 4 requires a promissory note to contain an unconditional undertaking to pay. "I.O.U. ₹8,000" only acknowledges a debt; it contains no promise to pay, so it is not a promissory note. Calling it a valid note is the trap: being signed by the debtor and stating an amount is not enough without the promise. It is not a bill or cheque either, as it contains no order to pay. In practice: lenders use a properly worded, stamped promissory note, such as "I promise to pay…", rather than an IOU slip.

mcqs.q: Who among these can issue a promissory note payable to bearer?
options: The RBI (or the Central Government as permitted)
mcqs.explain: Section 31 of the RBI Act, 1934 says only the Reserve Bank of India, or the Central Government where authorised (for example for one-rupee notes), may issue a promissory note payable to bearer on demand. If private persons could do this, they could create their own currency. "Any scheduled bank" is the trap: banks issue drafts and cheques, but cannot issue bearer notes. In practice: this is why only RBI notes, which are bearer promissory notes, circulate as money in India.

mcqs.q: The minimum number of distinct persons needed for a bill of exchange is:
mcqs.explain: Section 5 names three roles in a bill of exchange: drawer (who orders payment), drawee (who is ordered to pay) and payee (who receives payment). One person may fill two roles, for example the drawer may also be the payee, so the minimum number of distinct persons is two. Three is the trap: it counts roles, not people. One is wrong because drawer and drawee must differ for an order to make sense. In practice: a seller often draws a bill on a buyer payable "to me or my order".

mcqs.q: Which instrument requires acceptance?
mcqs.explain: A bill of exchange is an order by the drawer to the drawee, so the drawee becomes liable only after accepting it. A bill payable after sight must be presented for acceptance to fix its maturity. A promissory note is the trap: the maker signs a promise himself, so no acceptance is needed. Cheques are drawn on a bank and are payable on demand without acceptance. In practice: exporters send usance bills through banks to overseas buyers for acceptance before the goods are released.

mcqs.q: A cheque, by definition, includes:
options: Electronic cheques and images of truncated cheques
A promissory note drawn on a bank
A bill payable after sight drawn on a bank
A demand draft drawn on a person
mcqs.explain: Section 6 defines a cheque as a bill drawn on a named bank and payable only on demand. After the 2002 amendment, it also includes an electronic cheque and the electronic image of a truncated cheque. A bill payable after sight drawn on a bank is the trap: a cheque must be payable on demand, not after sight. A promissory note is a promise, not an order. In practice: under the Cheque Truncation System, banks clear cheques using images, and those images are legally cheques.

mcqs.q: A bill drawn in Nagpur on a merchant in Nairobi and accepted payable in Nairobi is:
mcqs.explain: Sections 11 and 12: an inland instrument is drawn or made in India and is either payable in India or drawn on a person resident in India. Any other instrument is foreign. This bill is drawn in Nagpur, but on a merchant in Nairobi and payable in Nairobi, so it is foreign. "Inland" is the trap: being drawn in India alone is not enough. In practice: exporters' bills drawn on overseas buyers are foreign bills, so the protest requirement for dishonour of foreign bills applies to them.

mcqs.q: Where an instrument may be construed either as a note or a bill, the holder:
options: May elect to treat it as either, and it is treated accordingly thereafter
Must treat it as a bill
Must treat it as a note
mcqs.explain: Section 17: an instrument that could be read as a note or equally as a bill is ambiguous. The holder may elect to treat it as either, and once he has elected, it is treated that way from then on. "Must treat it as a bill" is the trap: the law gives the holder the choice. The instrument stays enforceable. In practice: a bill where the drawer and drawee are the same person, such as a bank drawing on itself, is often treated as a promissory note.

mcqs.q: An instrument payable to order is negotiated by:
mcqs.explain: Section 48: an instrument payable to order is negotiated by the holder indorsing it and delivering it. Both steps are needed. "Delivery only" is the trap: that is how a bearer instrument is negotiated, under Section 47. Indorsement without delivery passes nothing, and banks do not register transfers of instruments. In practice: when a business passes a customer's order cheque to a supplier, it signs on the back with the supplier's name, then hands it over.

mcqs.q: Under Section 138, the payee must send a written notice of demand within ___ of receiving information of dishonour, and the drawer must pay within ___ of receiving it.
mcqs.explain: Section 138 proviso: the payee must send a written demand notice to the drawer within 30 days of receiving information from the bank that the cheque was returned unpaid. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving the notice to pay. "15 days; 30 days" is the trap: the two periods are simply reversed. In practice: lawyers diarise the date of the bank's return memo and send the notice by registered post and email well within 30 days, keeping proof of delivery.
mcqs.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)

mcqs.q: A cheque for ₹75,000 is dishonoured for insufficiency of funds and all conditions of Section 138 are met. The maximum fine is:
mcqs.explain: Section 138: dishonour of a cheque for insufficient funds is punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or a fine of up to twice the cheque amount, or both. For ₹75,000, the maximum fine is 2 × ₹75,000 = ₹1,50,000. ₹75,000 is the trap: it is only the cheque amount, once. ₹2,25,000 is three times the amount. In practice: courts often order compensation to the payee out of the fine, so complainants claim up to twice the cheque amount.
mcqs.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)

mcqs.q: Which cheque, if dishonoured, does NOT attract Section 138?
options: A cheque given to a sister as a birthday gift
A post-dated cheque for a loan instalment
mcqs.explain: Section 138 applies only to a cheque issued to discharge, wholly or partly, a legally enforceable debt or other liability. A cheque given as a birthday gift discharges no debt, so its dishonour is not an offence under Section 138. A post-dated cheque is the trap: it is covered once it falls due, because it is still issued against a debt. Rent and goods are clearly debts. In practice: in a Section 138 complaint, the accused often argues that no enforceable debt existed, so payees keep invoices or loan papers ready.
mcqs.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)

mcqs.q: A drawee to whom a bill is presented for acceptance may ask for time to consider of:
mcqs.explain: Section 63: when a bill is presented for acceptance, the drawee is allowed 48 hours, not counting public holidays, to decide whether to accept. 24 hours is the trap: it halves the period. "3 days including holidays" and 7 days are simply wrong periods. In practice: when a bank presents an export bill to an importer, it allows this time before treating the bill as dishonoured by non-acceptance.

mcqs.q: An indorser who has paid ₹1,00,000 on a dishonoured bill recovers it 6 months later from a prior party. Interest he can claim under Section 117 is:
mcqs.explain: Section 117(b): an indorser who has paid on a dishonoured instrument can recover the amount paid plus interest at 18% a year from the date of payment. For 6 months: ₹1,00,000 × 18% × 6/12 = ₹9,000. ₹18,000 is the trap: it charges a full year's interest. ₹6,000 uses 12%. In practice: when bills are discounted with banks and dishonoured, banks recover the bill amount with interest and charges from the drawer or indorsers.

questions.q: Define a promissory note. State its essential characteristics and distinguish it from a bill of exchange.

model.text: Section 4: a promissory note is a written instrument, not being a bank note or currency note, in which the maker, over his signature, undertakes without condition to pay a fixed sum of money only, to a definite person or his order, or to bearer (subject to the RBI Act).

items: In writing; express promise to pay (not a mere acknowledgment).
Maker and payee certain and different.

remarks: Most candidates write the distinction well but lose marks on essentials such as "money only" and "certain sum".
mistakes: Saying a promissory note can be payable to bearer by anyone.
Calling an IOU a promissory note.
tips: Three parts — three headings. Use a table for the distinction.

questions.q: Mehul gives Naveen a post-dated cheque dated 20 August for ₹2,40,000 towards repayment of a loan. On 18 August Mehul instructs his bank to stop payment, as his account balance is only ₹40,000. Naveen presents the cheque on 25 August; it is returned "payment stopped by drawer". Naveen sends a notice on 5 September (received on 8 September); Mehul does not pay. Mehul argues that the cheque was dishonoured for "stop payment", not for insufficiency of funds, so Section 138 does not apply. Advise Naveen.

model.provision: Section 138: dishonour of a cheque drawn for discharge of a legally enforceable debt, for insufficiency of funds (or exceeding the arrangement), is an offence if it is presented within three months or its validity, notice of demand is given within 30 days of information, and the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of the notice. A post-dated cheque is treated as drawn on the date it bears. Courts have held that a "stop payment" return where the account lacks funds is covered. Section 139 presumes the cheque was for a debt; Section 140 bars the defence that the drawer did not expect dishonour.
model.facts: The cheque was for repaying a loan (an enforceable debt). It was dated 20 August and presented on 25 August. Payment was stopped when the balance was only ₹40,000. Notice was sent on 5 September and received on 8 September; no payment followed.
model.analysis: Presentment was within three months of 20 August. The notice was within 30 days of the return. The 15-day period from 8 September expired on 23 September without payment. The stop-payment instruction was given because funds were insufficient, so Mehul cannot escape liability by using that label. The presumption under Section 139 also operates against him.
model.conclusion: Section 138 is attracted. Naveen can file a complaint; Mehul is liable to imprisonment up to two years, or fine up to ₹4,80,000, or both.

scheme.pt: Post-dated cheque date; stop payment with insufficient funds covered; Ss. 139/140
Application of dates (3 months, 30 days, 15 days)

remarks: Strong answers check each time limit against the dates given.
mistakes: Accepting the "stop payment" argument without looking at the account balance.
Counting three months from the date of handing over instead of the date on the cheque.
tips: A small date table inside the Analysis makes the answer easy to mark.

questions.q: Explain "inland instrument" and "foreign instrument" with one example each. How is the liability of parties to a foreign instrument determined?

model.text: Inland instrument (Section 11): a note, bill or cheque that originates in India and is either payable in India or drawn on someone residing in India. Example: a bill drawn in Lucknow on a trader in Patna. It remains inland even if indorsed abroad.
Foreign instrument (Section 12): any instrument that is not inland. Example: a bill drawn in Bhopal on a buyer in Tokyo, payable in Tokyo; or a note made in New York.
Liability (Section 134): unless the parties agree otherwise, the maker or drawer is bound by the law of the country of making, and the acceptor or indorser by the law of the country of payment.

remarks: Examples must be checked against both limbs of Section 11.
mistakes: Calling a bill drawn in India on a resident of India, payable abroad, a foreign bill.
tips: Test every example: made in India? payable in India OR drawee resident in India?

questions.q: State the circumstances in which presentment for payment of a negotiable instrument is not necessary.

items: The maker, drawee or acceptor deliberately blocks presentment; or he shuts his business premises (where the instrument is payable there) during business hours on a working day; or, being payable elsewhere, neither he nor anyone authorised attends there during business hours; or, not payable at a specified place, he cannot be found after due search [Section 76(a)].
As against a party who has engaged to pay notwithstanding non-presentment [76(b)].

As against a party who, after maturity and with knowledge of non-presentment, makes part payment, promises to pay in whole or part, or otherwise waives his right to take advantage of the default [76(c)].
As against the drawer, if he could not suffer damage from want of presentment [76(d)].
Also: no presentment is needed to charge the maker of a note payable on demand and not payable at a specified place [Section 64].

scheme.pt: Prevention / closure / non-attendance / cannot be found
Part payment / promise / waiver after maturity

remarks: Candidates often forget the drawer-suffers-no-damage case.
mistakes: Listing presentment rules (time, place) instead of the exceptions.
tips: Quote Section 76 and number the cases.

questions.q: Om tears a completed promissory note payable to Pia into two halves, sends one half to Pia by post and says he will send the other half after Pia pays him a commission. Pia demands that the note be treated as made and delivered. Advise.

model.provision: Section 46: making, acceptance or indorsement of a negotiable instrument is completed only by delivery, actual or constructive. Delivery must be voluntary and intended to pass the property in the instrument; delivery conditionally or for a special purpose does not pass it as between the immediate parties.
model.facts: Om sent only half of the note and withheld the other half, making its completion subject to a condition (payment of commission).
model.analysis: Sending half the note is not delivery of the instrument; Om has not parted with control of the complete document. Even if treated as delivery, it was conditional and, as between immediate parties, the condition can be shown.
model.conclusion: The making of the note is not complete. Pia cannot treat it as a delivered promissory note and cannot sue on it.

remarks: The point tested is that delivery completes the instrument.
mistakes: Treating the note as complete because it was fully written and signed.
tips: Start with "Delivery is essential" — it is the whole answer.

summary: Section 13: notes, bills, cheques payable to order or bearer; others negotiable by custom (hundis, treasury bills, bearer debentures).
Characteristics: writing, signature, free transferability, title free from defects, unconditional promise/order, money only, certainty, delivery.

Note (s.4): promise, 2 parties, no acceptance, not payable to bearer. Bill (s.5): order, 3 parties, acceptance, not bearer on demand. Cheque (s.6): bill on a specified banker, on demand; includes truncated and electronic cheques.
Inland (s.11): made in India + payable in India or drawn on a resident; foreign (s.12) otherwise; s.134 governing law.
Inchoate (s.20): signed blank stamped paper delivered — HDC recovers amount filled in (within stamp); others only intended amount. Ambiguous (s.17): holder elects.
Negotiation (s.14): bearer by delivery (s.47); order by indorsement and delivery (s.48); delivery essential (s.46); s.57 legal representative.

Section 138: enforceable debt + dishonour for funds + presented within 3 months/validity + notice within 30 days + no payment within 15 days → up to 2 years / fine up to 2× / both. s.139 presumption; s.140 no "did not expect" defence.

Presentment: s.61 acceptance (after sight), s.63 48 hours, s.64 payment, s.65 hours, s.66 maturity, s.67 instalments, ss.68–71 place, ss.72–74 cheques and demand instruments, s.75A excuse, s.76 unnecessary, s.77 banker's negligence.
Section 117: amount + expenses; indorser who paid → 18% p.a. interest from payment; exchange rate; may draw a bill for the compensation.
remember: 30 days for notice, 15 days to pay; complaint possible after that.
Drawee may take 48 hours to decide on acceptance.
traps: An IOU is not a promissory note.
A bill can be payable to bearer, but never to bearer on demand.
A cheque given as a gift or donation does not attract Section 138.
An inland bill stays inland even if indorsed abroad.

viva.q: What are the essential characteristics of a negotiable instrument?
viva.model: A negotiable instrument must be in writing and signed. It is freely transferable any number of times, and a holder in due course gets a title free from defects. It contains an unconditional promise or order to pay money only, the amount, time and payee must be certain, and it must be delivered.

viva.model: A promissory note contains a promise to pay, made by the debtor, and has two parties, the maker and the payee; it needs no acceptance and cannot be made payable to bearer. A bill of exchange contains an order to pay, made by the creditor, and has three parties, drawer, drawee and payee; it needs acceptance by the drawee.

cases.title: An export bill from Coimbatore
cases.case: Lakshmi Spinners of Coimbatore sold yarn to Hanoi Fabrics, Vietnam, and drew a bill of exchange in Coimbatore on Hanoi Fabrics for US$ 40,000, payable 60 days after sight in Hanoi. Hanoi Fabrics accepted it. Lakshmi indorsed the bill to its bank in Coimbatore, which took it in good faith for value. At maturity Hanoi Fabrics did not pay.

mcqs.q: The bill is:
options: A foreign bill — drawn in India but on a person abroad and payable abroad
An inland bill — drawn in India
An inland bill — indorsed in India
mcqs.explain: Sections 11 and 12: an instrument is inland only if drawn or made in India and either payable in India or drawn on a person resident in India. The bill was drawn in Coimbatore, but on a buyer in Vietnam and payable in Hanoi, so it is foreign. "Inland, drawn in India" is the trap: drawing in India is only half the test. Indorsement in India does not change the classification. In practice: exporters' bills are foreign bills, so banks handle them under foreign exchange rules and, on dishonour, arrange protest abroad.

mcqs.q: Which fact decides that the bill needed presentment for acceptance?
options: It is payable at a period after sight
It is drawn in US dollars
It was indorsed to a bank
It was drawn on a foreign buyer
mcqs.explain: Section 61: a bill payable after sight must be presented to the drawee for acceptance, because its maturity date runs from sight (acceptance or noting). This bill was "60 days after sight", so acceptance was needed to fix the due date. "Drawn in US dollars" is the trap: the currency has nothing to do with presentment for acceptance. Indorsement to a bank and a foreign drawee do not decide it either. In practice: banks collecting usance export bills present them to the importer's bank for acceptance before releasing shipping documents.

mcqs.q: Under Section 134, Lakshmi Spinners' liability as drawer is governed by the law of:
options: India, where it drew the bill
The country chosen by the bank
Whichever law gives the higher interest
mcqs.explain: Section 134: unless agreed otherwise, a drawer's or maker's liability on a foreign instrument is decided by the law of the place where it was made. The liability of the acceptor and indorser is governed by the law of the place where it is payable. Lakshmi drew the bill in India, so Indian law governs its liability. "Vietnam, where it is payable" is the trap: that rule applies to the acceptor, not the drawer. In practice: export finance teams check both laws when chasing payment across borders.

mcqs.q: The bank, as holder, claims from Lakshmi Spinners. Under Section 117 it is entitled to:
options: The amount due plus expenses of presenting, noting and protesting, at the current rate of exchange where applicable
Only the face value with no expenses
Face value plus a penalty of twice the amount
Nothing, as only the acceptor is liable
mcqs.explain: Section 117: the holder can recover from any party liable the amount due, plus the expenses properly incurred in presenting, noting and protesting the bill. Where the party charged lives at a place where the bill was payable in another currency, the amount is converted at the current rate of exchange. "Face value plus twice the amount" is the trap: that confuses this with the fine under Section 138. In practice: banks debit exporters' accounts with the bill amount plus foreign bank charges and protest fees.

cases.title: Orion Traders' bounced cheque
cases.case: Orion Traders bought furniture worth ₹4,80,000 from Zenith Interiors and gave a cheque dated 10 January for that amount. Zenith presented it on 2 March; it was returned on 4 March for "insufficient funds". Zenith received the return memo on 6 March, sent a demand notice on 20 March, which Orion received on 23 March. Orion paid nothing.

mcqs.q: The cheque falls within Section 138 because it was issued:
options: For discharge of a legally enforceable debt (price of goods)
As a security without any existing liability
mcqs.explain: Section 138 applies only to a cheque issued to discharge a legally enforceable debt or liability. Orion gave the cheque to pay for furniture it bought, which is a debt enforceable by Zenith. So dishonour for insufficient funds is covered. "As a gift" is the trap: a gift cheque creates no enforceable debt and is outside Section 138. In practice: a supplier filing a Section 138 complaint attaches the invoice and delivery proof to show the debt behind the cheque.
mcqs.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)

mcqs.q: Was the notice in time?
options: Yes — sent within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour on 6 March
No — it should have been sent within 15 days
No — it should have been sent before presentment
Yes — notice can be sent at any time
mcqs.explain: Under the Section 138 proviso, the payee must send a demand notice within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour from the bank. Zenith received the return memo on 6 March and sent notice on 20 March: 20 − 6 = 14 days, within 30. The cheque dated 10 January was also presented within its three-month validity. "Within 15 days" is the trap: 15 days is the drawer's time to pay after notice. In practice: lawyers count from the date the return memo is received, not the date of dishonour.
mcqs.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)

mcqs.q: On which date does the cause of action arise if Orion does not pay?
mcqs.explain: Orion received notice on 23 March, and has 15 days to pay. Counting from 24 March, the 15 days end on 7 April (8 days in March + 7 in April). The offence is complete on failure to pay within those 15 days, so the cause of action arises the next day, 8 April. "7 April" is the trap: the drawer still has that whole day to pay. In practice: the complaint must then be filed within one month of the cause of action arising, so counsel diarises 8 April carefully.
mcqs.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)

mcqs.q: The maximum fine that can be imposed is:
mcqs.explain: Section 138 allows a fine of up to twice the cheque amount, imprisonment up to two years, or both. For a cheque of ₹4,80,000: 2 × ₹4,80,000 = ₹9,60,000. ₹4,80,000 is the trap: it is only the cheque amount. ₹14,40,000 is three times the amount. In practice: magistrates often direct that much of the fine be paid to the complainant as compensation, which is why businesses use Section 138 to recover dues.
mcqs.topic: Dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds (Sections 138 to 140)
